source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

candidates.name: FirstOrderPivot
candidates.quote: A pivot high is a bar that has a higher high than the bar that came before it and the bar that comes after it... A pivot low is the same concept inverted.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: the bar one bar ago is a first-order swing pivot -- its low (long) is below both the low two bars ago and the current bar's low, i.e. a bar lower than both neighbors. Confirmed one bar after it forms (needs the following bar to know the neighbor exists). Short side is the mirrored pivot high, used as a resistance point.

complexity.reason: a bare three-bar comparison of prices on fixed offsets

notes: This is the book's foundational primitive; almost every later swing/pullback/channel/measured-move candidate in this book and in later chapters depends on it. The book calls it a 'first-order pivot' or 'swing high/low'.

candidates.name: HigherOrderPivot
candidates.quote: Second-order pivot highs (also called intermediate-term pivots) are first-order pivot highs that are preceded and followed by lower first-order pivot highs... most of our focus is on third-order pivots, which usually mark major inflections.
candidates.description: Recursive pivot-of-pivot: a first-order pivot (G01-01) of order K is a K-th-order pivot if it is preceded and followed by lower-order pivots of order K-1 that are themselves lower (for a low) or higher (for a high). The book uses order 2 (second-order/intermediate-term) and order 3 (third-order/major) as the practically useful levels. There is no rule that pivots of a given order must alternate high/low/high/low; runs of three or more same-type pivots in a row are possible and must be handled.
candidates.pseudocode: isPivotOfOrder(k, i) := if k == 1 then isFirstOrderPivot(i) else nearestPriorPivotOfOrder(k-1, i) is lower AND nearestNextPivotOfOrder(k-1, i) is lower  // long/low form; mirrored for highs

complexity.reason: needs a maintained list of already-identified lower-order pivots and a search over that list -- not a fixed-window loop, and pivots do not have to alternate

notes: The book explicitly disclaims predictive power: 'this is a backward-looking analytical method... it offers fantastic explanations of past market action, but has little or no predictive power at the right edge.' Kept as a structure/context primitive, not a trade trigger by itself.

candidates.name: ImpulseMoveOutOfEquilibrium
candidates.quote: Eventually, there is a failure of liquidity on one side, and the market makes a sudden, large movement in one direction... this type of sharp movement is called an impulse move or a momentum move.
candidates.description: A sharp, large-range directional move that breaks a market out of a quiet, range-bound (equilibrium) state -- the trigger event the book treats as the start of a possible trend. No numeric threshold is given in this chapter for 'sudden' or 'large'; a natural proxy is a bar (or short run of bars) whose range or net move exceeds a multiple of recent average range/ATR after a period of contraction.

complexity.reason: the concept is real and named ('impulse move') but Grimes gives no numeric threshold in this chapter; both the contraction test and the impulse-size test need a design decision before this is codeable

notes: This is the qualitative seed of the whole book's trend-structure chapters (3, 5); kept research-grade rather than rejected because Grimes treats it as the mechanical trigger of the whole market cycle.

candidates.name: SwingLegLengthAsymmetryShowsControl
candidates.quote: When buyers are stronger than sellers, upswings will be longer, both in price and in time, than downswings. When sellers are in control, downswings will be longer than upswings.
candidates.description: Context filter: over the recent swing structure, the average (or most recent) up-leg (pivot low to pivot high) is longer in price and duration than the average down-leg -- read as buyers in control (long context); mirrored for sellers in control.

complexity.reason: needs pivot detection (G01-01/G01-02) plus tracking and averaging leg lengths across the recent swing history

notes: Chapter 2's 'four trades' and Chapter 3's trend-structure chapter both build directly on this asymmetry idea.

candidates.name: HigherLowsIntoResistancePrecedeBreakout
candidates.quote: If buyers are able to hold the market higher on successive declines, a pattern of higher pivot lows pressing against the resistance area will result. This suggests real buying conviction supporting the move and the potential breakout.
candidates.description: Context filter that precedes the best breakouts: a run of successive pivot lows (G01-01) each higher than the last, occurring while price presses against a stable resistance level (recent range high). Mirrored: a run of successive lower pivot highs pressing against a support floor precedes the best downside breakouts.
candidates.pseudocode: pivotLow[k] > pivotLow[k+1] for k = 0..(numHigherLows-1) AND highest(high, rangeLookback) is roughly flat over that span

complexity.reason: needs pivot detection plus counting a rising sequence of pivot lows and a check that the resistance ceiling is stable

notes: Same figure/example recurs in Chapter 2's 'Support or Resistance Breaking' trade description (page 61) -- the dedup pass should merge with that chapter's version of this candidate.

candidates.name: InsideBar
candidates.quote: One simple way to quantify volatility contraction is by looking for inside bars, which are bars whose entire range is enclosed within the range of the previous bar.
candidates.description: The current bar's high is at or below the previous bar's high and its low is at or above the previous bar's low -- a single-bar volatility-contraction signal.

complexity.reason: a bare two-bar comparison of prices on fixed offsets

notes: Restates the corpus's existing InsideBar rule; recorded per the dedup-hint convention.

candidates.name: MultipleInsideBarsContractionBreakout
candidates.quote: A series of multiple inside bars on one time frame usually contains a triangle on the lower time frame... they can set up good breakouts with expectations for strong, extended moves away from the pattern.
candidates.description: N consecutive inside bars (G01-06), read as a volatility-contraction 'triangle' that favors a directional breakout away from the range once it resolves; a context filter for the breakout entry, not itself an entry.

complexity.reason: a fixed-length window loop counting a per-bar condition

notes: Grimes: 'Trading within triangles is usually a losing proposition... but they can set up good breakouts' -- i.e. this is a filter for a subsequent breakout entry, not a standalone entry signal.

candidates.name: CloseNearBarExtremeShowsConviction
candidates.quote: a close near the high of the bar usually shows that buyers were in control going into the end of the time period. Conversely, closes near the middle of the bar... show a certain neutrality and lack of conviction.
candidates.description: The close sits in the upper fraction of the bar's own high-low range (long: buyer conviction); mirrored for a close near the low (seller conviction).

candidates.name: ConsecutiveClosesAtBarHighExhaustionWarning
candidates.quote: several bars in a row close on their absolute highs. Many traders would assume that this is indicative of a very strong market, but, statistically, this condition more often indicates short-term exhaustion and at least a slight reversal -- be careful of entering with the trend after several bars close on their highs.
candidates.description: N consecutive bars each closing at (or within a small tolerance of) its own bar high is read as a short-term exhaustion warning rather than confirmation of strength -- a filter meant to block/discourage a fresh with-trend entry, not itself a reversal entry.
candidates.pseudocode: count(closeIsAtBarHigh, lag=0..(consecutiveBars-1)) == consecutiveBars  where closeIsAtBarHigh := (high[lag]-close[lag]) <= closeToHighToleranceAtrFraction * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: a window loop with a per-bar tolerance test and a persistent count of consecutive occurrences

notes: Distinct from ConsecutiveUpBars (close above own open) -- this tests close proximity to the bar's own high, not the open/close relationship.

candidates.name: LargeRangeBarRelativeToRecent
candidates.quote: Large bars relative to recent bars on one time frame most likely contain trends on the lower time frame... Small bars on one time frame are probably trading ranges on lower time frames.
candidates.description: The current bar's range is large relative to recent bars' ranges, read as evidence the (unobserved) lower time frame inside this bar trended; a small bar reads as an LTF trading range. A multi-timeframe-inference idea approximated on the single observed timeframe as a plain range-vs-recent-average test.
notes: The book's actual claim (that a large HTF bar implies a lower-timeframe trend) cannot be verified from the bars the engine sees; only the size comparison itself is mechanizable.

candidates.name: FailureTestAtNewExtreme
candidates.quote: There are multiple failure tests above the highs, as the market spikes to new extremes and is unable to find the buying pressure to support itself there.
candidates.description: The bar makes a new high beyond the recent swing high but closes back inside the prior range (fails to hold the extreme) -- an early warning of loss of trend momentum. Mirrored at new lows.
candidates.pseudocode: high[0] > highest(high[1], lookback) AND close[0] < highest(high[1], lookback)

complexity.reason: a window-max lookup plus a close comparison against that computed level

candidates.name: ShrinkingSwingHighIncrements
candidates.quote: Each bar continues to make a higher high up into mid-April, but at a declining rate. We could characterize these as 'reluctant highs,' to indicate waning momentum.
candidates.description: Successive new swing/pivot highs are each made by a smaller margin over the prior high than the margin before it -- a momentum-loss warning ('reluctant highs'). Mirrored for declining lows in a downtrend.

complexity.reason: needs pivot detection plus comparing successive pivot-to-pivot increments

candidates.name: ShrinkingBarRangeSequence
candidates.quote: the bars are becoming smaller, indicating that trading interest is drying up, and there are no more large trend bars... in April.
candidates.description: Bar ranges over a recent window are shrinking bar to bar -- a trend-exhaustion/momentum-loss warning, paired with G01-12 in the book's example.

complexity.reason: a short run of consecutive bar-range comparisons

candidates.name: HighAndTightFlagPullback
candidates.quote: one or two small bars that hold near the extreme of a trend leg (near the lows in a downtrend or the highs in an uptrend) are often a complete lower time frame pullback. As such, these simple one- or two-bar pullbacks (high and tight flags) are tradable structures in very strong trends.
candidates.description: In a strong uptrend, one or two consecutive small-range bars that hold near the most recent swing high (rather than making a deep retracement) constitute a complete, tradable pullback; mirrored near swing lows in a downtrend.
candidates.pseudocode: isUptrend(...) AND count(isSmallBarNearRecentHigh, lag=0..(pullbackBars-1)) == pullbackBars  where isSmallBarNearRecentHigh := (high[lag]-low[lag]) < smallBarAtrFraction*atr(atrLookback) AND (highest(high[1],swingLookback) - low[lag]) < nearAtrFraction*atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: needs an uptrend test, pivot/swing-high detection, and a multi-bar small-range-near-extreme window test

notes: Chapter 3 (mined separately) is expected to give the precise, general pullback taxonomy; this is Chapter 1's specific example of the shallowest form.

candidates.name: ComplexPullbackThreeLegStructure
candidates.quote: Another important pullback pattern in an uptrend has several bars with downward closes separated by a single bar with an upward close... From that second leg, the market turns down again to make another countertrend leg that is usually approximately as long as the first one.
candidates.description: A complex, two-legged countertrend pullback in an uptrend: a run of down-closing bars, then one bar closing up (a small failed resumption attempt), then a second down-closing leg of roughly the same length/depth as the first. Mirrored for a downtrend.
candidates.pseudocode: downLegLength(leg1) > 0 AND upBarsBetween == 1 AND downLegLength(leg2) approximately equals downLegLength(leg1)  // 'approximately equals' left as a tolerance parameter

complexity.reason: needs run-length counting for two legs plus a tolerance comparison between their lengths, and 'approximately as long' is not numerically specified

notes: Chapter 3 (mined separately, 'Trading Complex Pullbacks' is actually Chapter 6) is expected to define this precisely; this is Chapter 1's informal preview, kept per the high-recall instruction.

candidates.name: AtrMultipleZigzagSwingReversal
candidates.quote: it is also possible to define the reversal with other tools, such as reversing a specific multiple of the average range off the previous swing... Assume now that the market falls back to $63.00, which exceeds the $1.00 reversal threshold, so now a short horizontal line is plotted.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: a zigzag/swing-chart pivot defined by a minimum reversal amount off the running extreme since the last confirmed swing point, rather than by neighboring-bar comparisons (G01-01). Grimes's own example uses a fixed dollar reversal (a price-level constant, rejected by the shift test); he explicitly also allows the reversal to be defined as a multiple of average range (ATR), which is used here instead.
candidates.pseudocode:
runningExtremeSinceLastSwing = highest(high, sinceLastSwing)  // long form: watching for a down-reversal off a running high
zigzagReversal = (runningExtremeSinceLastSwing - close[0]) > reversalAtrMultiple * atr(atrLookback)

complexity.reason: needs a running extreme tracked since the last confirmed swing point (state that persists across a variable number of bars), not a fixed window

notes: The book's literal example is a $1.00 fixed reversal (rejected by the shift test as a price-level constant); re-expressed here in ATR units per the shift-test convention, with the original dollar figure kept for reference. This is an alternative pivot-detection primitive to G01-01/G01-02 (neighbor-comparison pivots), useful where a smoother, threshold-based swing definition is wanted.

rejected.quote: E(X) = x1 p1 + x2 p2 + ... + xk pk ... the definition of an edge is simple: can you properly identify entry and exit points in the market so that, over a large sample size, the sum of the profit and loss (P&L) from your winning trades is greater than the sum of your losing trades?
rejected.reason: expectancy/probability-theory background and the abstract definition of a trading edge -- no bar-level test

rejected.quote: You are certainly not the best-capitalized player in the arena... One solution is to focus on the three-day to two-week swings, as many swing traders do.
rejected.reason: discretionary commentary on why small traders can compete with institutions and choice of holding period -- no bar-level test

rejected.quote: Modern software packages are a mixed blessing for traders... Keep the same format between all markets and time frames, and keep the setup of all of your charts as consistent as possible.
rejected.reason: chart-setup and workflow advice (consistency, avoiding indicator clutter) -- no bar-level test

rejected.quote: In these cases, the vertical axis of the chart should be scaled logarithmically... any time you have greater than a 100 percent price increase on a chart, and for any chart showing more than two years of data.
rejected.reason: chart display convention (linear vs. log scale); the '100 percent price increase' threshold is itself a condition on a price LEVEL (percent-of-price), not a difference, so would fail the shift test even if it were reframed as a trading rule

rejected.quote: In general, time frames should be related to each other by a factor of 3 to 5... if a trader has been trading a system on 5-minute charts with $0.25 stops and wishes to transfer that to 30-minute charts, the stops will probably need to be adjusted to about $0.61.
rejected.reason: meta-guidance for setting up multi-timeframe chart layouts and for rescaling stop sizes when switching timeframes -- not itself a bar-level trading condition

rejected.quote: Most traders today seem to be focused on using candlestick charts, but the more old-fashioned bar charts should not be overlooked... closing prices on intraday bars are essentially random samples and may differ from platform to platform.
rejected.reason: chart-type (bar vs. candle) and data-provider commentary -- no bar-level test

rejected.quote: There are many different indicators in common usage, and traders have a wide range of approaches and applications for these tools.
rejected.reason: general discretionary commentary on indicator use -- no specific bar-level test (specific indicators are mined individually elsewhere, e.g. Appendix B)

rejected.quote: Significant support and resistance levels are visible as rough areas (not precise lines) beyond which pivots have been unable to penetrate.
rejected.reason: preview of the support/resistance concept; developed with a precise, testable definition in Chapter 2's four-trades framework (this file) and in Chapter 4 (mined separately) -- not mined again here to avoid a vague duplicate

rejected.quote: A trader using this approach might look for wedges, pennants, flags, boxes, ledges, head and shoulders patterns, and double tops and bottoms... Richard Schabacker was the first writer to codify this approach.
rejected.reason: historical narrative about the two schools of technical analysis (Schabacker/Edwards & Magee vs. Wyckoff) -- no bar-level test

rejected.quote: consider the single candle in Figure 1.11 with an empty body... There are three things we know with certainty about this candle... Traders developing a sense for price action need to spend a lot of time contemplating all of the lower time frame scenarios that could produce each bar.
rejected.reason: an exercise in imagining possible lower-timeframe paths that could have produced one bar -- explicitly stated to be ambiguous ('in almost every case, there are multiple possibilities') and not reducible to a mechanical bar-level test

rejected.quote: I started trading in the 1990s, in the twilight years of the old, classic paper chart books... I would suggest that interested traders commit to doing this for a period of not less than two months.
rejected.reason: personal narrative and practice recommendation (drawing charts by hand) -- no bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 1 is mostly the book's argument that a verifiable statistical edge is necessary and an overview of chart-reading philosophy (consistency, scaling, time frames, indicators) -- all rejected as non-mechanical. Along the way it defines several primitives the rest of the book depends on: first-order and higher-order swing pivots (G01-01/02), an alternative ATR-threshold zigzag pivot (G01-16), and a cluster of bar-anatomy and momentum-loss examples (close position in range, consecutive closes at the high, shrinking swing increments, shrinking bar ranges, failure tests at new extremes) that substantially overlap with existing Brooks-corpus rules and are recorded with likely_existing_rule hints. It also gives the book's first informal preview of simple and complex pullback structure (G01-14, G01-15), which Chapter 3 (mined by a sibling agent) is expected to formalize -- the dedup pass should check those against whatever Chapter 3 produces.
